authoring_notes: Authored for the api-call branch content schema. Uses CompTIA's official objective IDs as skill IDs because the bullet examples under SY0-701 objectives are not separately numbered. Definition-first wording, short reveals, two- or three-column mobile-friendly tables, and varied retrieval/application practice are intentional. Ambiguous control-classification examples were avoided or explicitly described as context-dependent.

prompts.label: START HERE
prompts.placeholder: What are the two labels used to describe a control?

reveal.text: A security control is a safeguard that reduces risk. A category describes what kind of control it is, while a type describes the job the control performs.

prompts.label: TWO LABELS
prompts.placeholder: Compare the two taxonomies.

columns.title: Category
items: Technical
Managerial
Operational
Physical

columns.title: Type
items: Preventive
Deterrent
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
Directive

reveal.text: Category tells you what a control is. Type tells you what job it performs.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: A safeguard used to reduce security risk. It can be technical, procedural, managerial, or physical.

nodes.title: Technical, managerial, operational, and physical controls

prompts.label: WHAT ARE THE CATEGORIES?
prompts.placeholder: What makes the four categories different?

reveal.text: The four categories describe the nature of the control or how it is implemented: technology, management/governance, day-to-day people and process, or a physical safeguard.

cells.think: People carrying out a security process
Tangible protection of spaces or equipment

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: WHAT JOB DOES THE CONTROL DO?
prompts.placeholder: How do these three control types differ?

reveal.text: Preventive controls try to stop an unwanted event, deterrent controls try to discourage it, and detective controls identify that an event or condition occurred.

cells.job: Block or reduce the chance of an event

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: WHAT JOB DOES THE CONTROL DO?
prompts.placeholder: How do these three control types differ?

reveal.text: Corrective controls fix or restore after a problem. Compensating controls use an alternative safeguard, while directive controls tell people what they must do.

cells.job: Fix or recover after a problem
cells.example: Restore a compromised workstation from a clean image

cells.job: Reduce risk with an alternate safeguard
cells.example: Extra network isolation and monitoring for a legacy system
Policy that requires approved removable media

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: The same control can have more than one label

prompts.label: TWO WAYS TO DESCRIBE A CONTROL
prompts.placeholder: What is the difference between a control category and a control type?

reveal.text: Category and type answer different questions. Use the scenario to identify both instead of memorizing one permanent label for a control.

prompts.label: DON'T FORCE ONE LABEL
prompts.placeholder: Why can the same control appear under more than one label?

reveal.text: Category and type answer different questions. A control can have one category and one or more functions, so classify it from the scenario instead of memorizing a single permanent label.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

modules.title: Build the core security mental models

prompts.label: CIA TRIAD
prompts.placeholder: What does CIA protect?

reveal.text: The CIA triad is a three-part security goal: protect data from unauthorized disclosure, protect it from unauthorized change, and keep systems and data usable when needed.

cells.question: Who is allowed to see it?
Can authorized users reach it when needed?

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: AAA
prompts.placeholder: Which question does each A answer?

reveal.text: Authentication verifies an identity, authorization decides what that identity may do, and accounting records relevant activity for traceability.

cells.question: What are you allowed to do?
What did you do, and when?

cells.remember: Verify a human identity with evidence such as a password, passkey, token, or biometric factor.
Verify a device, service, or workload with machine credentials such as certificates or cryptographic keys.
Define how permissions are granted after identity is known, for example from roles, attributes, rules, or resource relationships.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: WHAT DOES IT MEAN?
prompts.placeholder: What problem does non-repudiation solve?

reveal.text: Non-repudiation provides evidence that makes it difficult for a party to credibly deny a recorded action or signature. Digital signatures are a common cryptographic mechanism that supports it.

prompts.label: NOT CONFIDENTIALITY
prompts.placeholder: What should you not confuse with non-repudiation?

reveal.text: A digital signature does not hide the message. It helps verify the signer and detect modification; encryption is what provides confidentiality.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST Digital Signatures

prompts.label: CURRENT VS. TARGET
prompts.placeholder: What two states are compared?

reveal.text: A gap analysis compares the current security state with a required or desired target state, then identifies what is missing.

prompts.label: USE THE GAP
prompts.placeholder: How do you turn a gap into an action plan?

items: Describe the current state
Define the target state
Identify the differences
Prioritize changes that close the important gaps

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: ZERO TRUST
prompts.placeholder: What changes when you stop trusting network location by default?

reveal.text: Zero Trust does not trust a user, device, or workload just because it is inside a network. Access is policy-driven and uses current context.

prompts.label: THINK IN THREE MOVES
prompts.placeholder: What should Zero Trust make you think about?

items: Use adaptive identity and context instead of a one-time perimeter decision.
Reduce threat scope with least privilege and smaller trust zones.
Apply policy-driven access decisions and re-evaluate when context changes.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture

nodes.title: Zero Trust: control plane and data plane

prompts.label: WHO DECIDES? WHO ENFORCES?
prompts.placeholder: Which components decide, execute, and enforce access?

reveal.text: Zero Trust separates access decisions from enforcement. The Policy Engine decides, the Policy Administrator carries out the decision, and the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) controls the access path.

cells.job: Decides to grant, deny, or revoke access
Executes the PE decision and establishes or terminates the path
Enforces the access decision at the resource boundary
Requests access to an enterprise resource

prompts.label: TRAFFIC FLOW
prompts.placeholder: Follow one access request.

items: Subject requests access
Policy Engine decides
Policy Administrator tells the PEP what to do
PEP allows or blocks access to the resource

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture

prompts.label: PHYSICAL SECURITY
prompts.placeholder: What is physical security protecting?

reveal.text: Physical security protects facilities, equipment, and people from unauthorized physical access, damage, or interference.

cells.examples: Security guard, access badge, video surveillance

cells.clue: Changes in infrared energy, often used for motion/heat detection
Weight or force on a surface
Movement detected through reflected radio-frequency energy
Movement detected through high-frequency sound reflections

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: A small controlled entry space, usually with two doors, that restricts passage into a protected area.

prompts.label: DECOYS
prompts.placeholder: Why deploy something fake on purpose?

reveal.text: Deception technology uses monitored decoys or fake data to make suspicious interaction visible. The decoy should not contain real production value.

cells.meaning: A decoy file intended to trigger attention when touched
Fake data or a credential-like token whose use is suspicious

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

modules.title: Make changes without creating security incidents

nodes.title: Change management protects security and availability

prompts.label: WHY MANAGE CHANGES?
prompts.placeholder: Why can a normal configuration change become a security problem?

reveal.text: Change management reduces the chance that a well-intended change causes an outage or weakens security. Common safeguards include review, testing, approval, recovery planning, and documentation.

prompts.label: COMMON SAFE FLOW
prompts.placeholder: Use this as a mental model, not a universal mandatory sequence.

items: Identify owner, stakeholders, scope, and impact
Test the change and record results
Obtain the required approval
Schedule an appropriate maintenance window
Implement and validate the change
Use the backout plan if needed
Update diagrams, policies, procedures, and version history

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: A person or group affected by, responsible for, or able to influence a change.
A prepared method for reversing or recovering from a change that causes unacceptable problems.
A planned period when a change may be performed, often when disruption is least harmful.

prompts.label: LOOK BEYOND THE ONE SETTING
prompts.placeholder: What should be checked before approving a security change?

reveal.text: Impact analysis asks what the change can affect before it reaches production: allowed or denied traffic, restricted activities, downtime, service or application restarts, legacy applications, and dependencies.

cells.question: Will legitimate or malicious traffic be allowed or blocked differently?
Does policy, regulation, or the environment prohibit part of the planned work?
Does the change require a restart, and what becomes unavailable?
Can the older application support the new setting or protocol?
Which other systems rely on this component or behavior?
How long can the service be unavailable, and who is affected?

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: A system, service, library, or process that another component relies on to work correctly.

nodes.title: Approval, ownership, test results, and recovery planning

prompts.label: WHAT IS CHANGE GOVERNANCE?
prompts.placeholder: What should change governance define before production work begins?

reveal.text: Change governance defines who owns and approves a change, what evidence is required, and how the team will recover if the change fails.

spans.text: who owns and approves a change

prompts.label: WHO AND WHAT MUST BE READY?

cells.purpose: Someone is accountable for the change and its outcome
Affected teams can review risks, dependencies, and timing
Evidence shows what happened before production rollout
The required authority accepts the planned change
There is a defined recovery path if the change fails
The change occurs at an approved time
Repeatable steps reduce improvisation and inconsistency

prompts.label: BEFORE PRODUCTION
prompts.placeholder: What should you be able to answer before rollout?

items: Know who owns the change.
Know who is affected.
Have test evidence and the required approval.
Know exactly how to recover if the change causes harm.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: A documented, repeatable procedure for carrying out a routine task consistently.

prompts.label: KEEP THE CURRENT STATE TRUE
prompts.placeholder: Why does documentation matter after the technical work is finished?

reveal.text: After an approved change, update diagrams and relevant policies or procedures so they describe the real environment. Version control preserves a reviewable history of document or configuration changes.

prompts.label: VERSION CONTROL IS NOT THE WHOLE BACKOUT PLAN
prompts.placeholder: What is the limit of version control?

reveal.text: Version control can restore a previous file revision, but a full backout may also require restoring services, data, dependencies, or infrastructure state.

prompts.label: POST-CHANGE CHECK
prompts.placeholder: What should be updated after the change?

items: Update diagrams.
Update policies and procedures when behavior changed.
Record the approved version and test/validation evidence.
Confirm that the environment matches the documented state.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: CHOOSE THE RIGHT KEY MODEL
prompts.placeholder: What is the biggest practical difference?

reveal.text: Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret and is efficient for bulk data. Asymmetric cryptography uses a public/private key pair for signatures, identity, and key establishment.

cells.best: Signatures, identity, and protecting key establishment
Create a session secret without using one long-term shared secret in advance

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management

glossary.definition: Readable data before encryption.
Encrypted output that should not be readable without the required key.
A temporary shared secret used to protect one communication session.

nodes.title: Encryption scope: disk, file, database, record, and transport

prompts.label: WHERE IS THE ENCRYPTION APPLIED?
prompts.placeholder: What does 'level' mean in this objective?

reveal.text: Encryption can protect different scopes. Choose the scope based on what must be protected: a device, storage unit, file, database value, or network communication.

cells.protects: The storage device at rest; protection is strongest when the device is locked or powered off
A selected storage partition or logical volume
Selected files instead of the entire device
A database or database storage layer
Data while it crosses a network connection

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management

prompts.label: HASHING IS NOT ENCRYPTION
prompts.placeholder: What can a hash do that encryption is not trying to do?

reveal.text: A cryptographic hash turns input into a fixed-size digest designed to be hard to reverse. Hashes support integrity checks and password-storage schemes, but not confidentiality.

cells.job: Adds a unique random value so identical passwords do not produce identical stored hashes and precomputed tables are less useful
Makes each password guess intentionally expensive
Stores a verifier instead of storing the plaintext password

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management

glossary.definition: The fixed-size output produced by a cryptographic hash function.
Key derivation function: a function that derives keying material from an input; password KDFs are designed to make password guessing more expensive.

reveal.text: A signer uses a private key to create a digital signature. A verifier uses the matching public key to check integrity and signer identity; the signature can also support non-repudiation.

prompts.label: NOT CONFIDENTIALITY
prompts.placeholder: What does a signature not provide by itself?

reveal.text: Signing does not hide the content. If confidentiality is also required, encryption is a separate operation.

prompts.label: PKI
prompts.placeholder: What makes PKI more than just one certificate?

reveal.text: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the people, policies, processes, and technology used to issue, manage, validate, and revoke public-key certificates.

prompts.label: TRUST CHAIN
prompts.placeholder: How does a public key become a trusted identity binding?

items: A subject controls a private key and corresponding public key
A certificate binds identity or a name to the public key
A certificate authority signs the certificate
A verifier builds trust toward a configured trust anchor

glossary.definition: A configured root of trust used as the starting point for certificate-path validation, commonly a trusted root CA certificate.

prompts.label: WHAT IS CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT?
prompts.placeholder: What problem do certificate requests, trust, and revocation solve?

reveal.text: Certificate lifecycle controls help request certificates, establish trust, and determine whether a certificate should still be accepted.

cells.meaning: Issues and signs certificates under a trust policy
A request containing a public key and identifying information that is sent to a CA
Signed by its own private key; not automatically trusted by other systems
Issued by a CA that relying systems may already trust
Covers multiple hostnames at a wildcard position, such as *.example.com
A configured trusted starting point used when validating a certificate chain, commonly a trusted root CA certificate

prompts.label: IS THE CERTIFICATE STILL VALID?
prompts.placeholder: Compare the two revocation-status methods.

columns.title: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)

columns.title: OCSP
items: An online status query for a certificate

glossary.definition: Marking a certificate as no longer trusted before its normal expiration date.

nodes.title: TPM, HSM, key management system, and secure enclave

prompts.label: WHY ARE THERE DIFFERENT KEY TOOLS?
prompts.placeholder: What do TPMs, HSMs, key management systems, and secure enclaves protect?

reveal.text: These tools protect cryptographic keys or sensitive operations in different places. Choose the tool based on where protection and key management are needed.

cells.mental: Endpoint hardware trust and protected key operations/storage tied to a platform
Dedicated tamper-resistant hardware that safeguards keys and performs cryptographic operations
Central control of key creation, access, rotation, use, and lifecycle
Isolated execution area that protects sensitive code or data from the rest of the system

prompts.label: CHOOSE BY BOUNDARY
prompts.placeholder: What clue points to each tool?

items: Need platform-bound device trust or protected endpoint keys: think TPM.
Need high-value keys and cryptographic operations inside dedicated protected hardware: think HSM.
Need centralized key lifecycle and access control: think key management system.
Need isolated execution inside a processor or system: think secure enclave.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management

glossary.definition: Replacing a cryptographic key with a new key according to policy or lifecycle needs.

nodes.title: Algorithm choice, key length, and key escrow

prompts.label: STRENGTH IS A PACKAGE
prompts.placeholder: Why is 'more bits' not the whole answer?

reveal.text: Cryptographic strength depends on the algorithm, key size, implementation, and key handling. Key lengths are not directly comparable across different algorithm families.

spans.text: algorithm, key size, implementation, and key handling

prompts.label: KEY ESCROW
prompts.placeholder: What trade-off does key escrow create?

reveal.text: Key escrow keeps a controlled recovery copy of a cryptographic key so an authorized recovery process can regain access when policy requires it. Escrow improves recoverability but creates another sensitive key location that must be protected.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management

glossary.definition: Controlled storage of a recovery copy of a cryptographic key for authorized recovery.

prompts.label: WHAT DO THESE DATA-HIDING METHODS DO?
prompts.placeholder: How are steganography, tokenization, and data masking related?

reveal.text: Steganography, tokenization, and data masking reduce exposure in different ways. They hide data, replace it, or conceal part of it.

cells.job: Hides the existence of data inside another carrier such as an image or audio file
Replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive token; the tokenization system keeps or derives the relationship to the original value
Hides or substitutes part of a value so the original is not fully exposed

prompts.label: NOT THE SAME AS ENCRYPTION
prompts.placeholder: Why should you not treat every hiding technique as encryption?

reveal.text: These techniques can reduce exposure, but they do not all provide the mathematical confidentiality guarantees of encryption. Choose the method that matches the data-handling goal.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: TAMPER-EVIDENT HISTORY
prompts.placeholder: What security property should blockchain make you think about?

reveal.text: A blockchain links records with cryptographic hashes and rules for adding entries. This can make history tamper-evident or tamper-resistant, but not automatically confidential.

prompts.label: PUBLIC DOES NOT MEAN SECRET
prompts.placeholder: What is the common trap with a public ledger?

reveal.text: An open public ledger is designed so ledger data can be independently observed or verified according to the system's rules. Public visibility and confidentiality are different properties.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

glossary.definition: Designed so unauthorized changes can be detected.
Designed to make unauthorized changes difficult, though not impossible.
